MA490 topic guides

MA490 Topic Guide

Measures and Probability Spaces

Use countable additivity to turn structure into calculations.

Purpose

State the measure and probability-space definitions, then prove standard consequences such as monotonicity, subadditivity and continuity.Exam use: Sigma-algebra domain, disjoint decomposition, monotone direction, finiteness and limiting set operation are shown.

Question plan

  1. Identify the measurable space (Ω,F).
  2. State non-negativity, null empty set and countable additivity exactly.
  3. Make unions disjoint before using additivity.
  4. For a limit of sets, rewrite it as disjoint increments.
  5. Question interpretation: For verify a measure, check empty set and countable additivity on disjoint families; for calculate, decompose into disjoint pieces before applying additivity.

Definitions

A measure μ:F→[0,∞] has μ(∅)=0 and is countably additive on disjoint sets. A probability measure additionally has μ(Ω)=1. A probability space is (Ω,F,P).Rapid recall: A measure mu maps a sigma-algebra to [0,infinity], has mu(empty)=0 and countable additivity; probability adds mu(Omega)=1; continuity from below always holds, while continuity from above needs finite measure of the first set.

Proof method

For continuity from below, set B1=A1 and Bn=An\An−1. The Bn are disjoint and their union is the increasing limit. Apply countable additivity.Exam workflow: Rewrite unions disjointly, apply additivity or continuity in the correct direction, and state any finiteness hypothesis before subtracting infinities.

Worked simple example

On Ω={1,2,3,4} with P({i})=1/4, P({1,2}∪{2,3})=3/4. Do not add 1/2+1/2 without removing the overlap.

Practice 1 — continuity from below from countable additivity [9 marks]

Prompt. For An↑A, prove μ(A)=lim μ(An) directly from countable additivity. Question-demand diagnosis. The increasing sequence must be converted to disjoint increments. Fastest route. Set B1=A1, Bn=An\An−1 and sum. Topic-specific trap. Additivity cannot be applied directly to the nested An.

If A_n increases to A, write B_1=A_1 and B_n=A_n minus A_{n-1}. The B_n are disjoint, A is their union, and A_N is union_{n<=N}B_n. Thus mu(A_N)=sum_{n<=N}mu(B_n) increases to sum_n mu(B_n)=mu(A). This proves continuity from below directly from countable additivity.

Graduated exam bridges

1. Basic: Show μ(A)≤μ(B) when A⊆B. Check: write B=A disjoint-union (B\A).

2. Exam: Derive countable subadditivity for arbitrary An. Check: replace An by disjoint new parts contained in An.

Practice 2 — continuity from above with finite initial measure [9 marks]

Prompt. If An↓ and μ(A1)<∞, prove μ(∩An)=lim μ(An). Question-demand diagnosis. The finite-measure hypothesis must be used when subtracting. Fastest route. Apply continuity from below to A1\An, then rearrange finite quantities. Topic-specific trap. ∞−∞ is undefined; omitting finiteness invalidates this proof.

Paper-style synthesis: for decreasing A_n with mu(A_1)<infinity, prove mu(intersection A_n)=lim mu(A_n). Check apply continuity from below to B_n=A_1 minus A_n, then use finite subtraction mu(B_n)=mu(A_1)-mu(A_n).

Mistakes

  • Using additivity for overlapping sets.
  • Forgetting that μ may be infinite.
  • Using continuity from above without a finite initial measure when required.
  • Recovery rule: Do not write infinity-infinity in a continuity-from-above proof; the finite first-measure hypothesis prevents it.

Checklist

  • I can distinguish a measurable space from a measure space.
  • I can disjointise a union.
  • I can state the finite-measure condition for continuity from above.
  • Final 60-second audit: Sigma-algebra domain, disjoint decomposition, monotone direction, finiteness and limiting set operation are shown.

Past-paper note

High confidence: definitions, subadditivity and continuity from below/above are repeated long-question targets. Back to paper evidence.
